clue.text: A mere puppet of Stravinsky

parts.note: the straw-filled puppet who comes to life as the hero of a Stravinsky ballet score of 1911

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that someone is nothing more than the composer's plaything.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the Ballets Russes piece is a fairground marionette brought to life.

clue.text: Woman counsellor shows rage that is unusual

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A female adviser loses her temper in an uncharacteristic way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' scrambles RAGE plus IE, the abbreviation of 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nymph who advised the Roman king Numa gave her name to any female adviser or mentor.

clue.text: It looked dull to Jane Eyres trifling taste

definitions.text: It looked dull to Jane Eyres trifling taste

parts.words: It looked dull to Jane Eyres trifling taste
parts.note: echoes the young heroine at Lowood, who glances at a book Helen Burns is reading and finds it dull to her 'trifling taste'

explanation.surface: A child dismisses a book as boring.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue adapts Jane's own words in chapter 5 of Charlotte Brontë's novel about the Samuel Johnson tale Helen Burns is reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's oriental moral fable is the book Helen Burns reads at Lowood school.

clue.text: Murray note revised astronomical measurement

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so the letters of these two words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An editor named Murray amends a memo about stargazing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges the ten letters of MURRAY NOTE.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the charting or measuring of stars and their positions, from the Greek for heaven plus measure.

clue.text: That man's conservative — a subject of 7

parts.note: a possessive for a male person, 'his'
a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Someone's political leanings are discussed as a topic for a French writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is MICHELET, the French historian, so his subject is the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Michelet wrote a vast account of France's past, so the study of past events was his field.

clue.text: Eponymous daughter of The Potteries

parts.note: the miser's daughter who gives her name to Arnold Bennett's 1902 novel set in the Staffordshire pottery towns

explanation.surface: A girl from the Staffordshire pottery district who gives her name to something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Potteries are the pottery-making towns around Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, Bennett's 'Five Towns'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bennett's novel is titled after its heroine, Anna Tellwright, of the Five Towns.

clue.text: Napoleon is the idol of the uneducated" ()

definitions.text: Napoleon is the idol of the uneducated" ()

parts.words: Napoleon is the idol of the uneducated" ()
parts.note: a quotation whose author is left blank for the solver to supply: the nineteenth-century French historian who wrote it

explanation.surface: A remark on the emperor's popularity among ordinary people, with its source left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: TLS quotation clues leave the empty brackets for the author; the clue numbering elsewhere calls this writer a historian.
explanation.definitionFit: The French historian Jules Michelet is credited with this judgement on Bonaparte's popular appeal.

clue.text: Drear panel rubbish C. S. Lewis work

indicators.note: used as a verb, to rubbish is to trash, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a dreary discussion panel about an Oxford author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbish' rearranges the ten letters of DREAR PANEL.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1943 novel set on Venus is the second book of Lewis's Space Trilogy.

clue.text: Catch sight of review

definitions.meaning: a critic's write-up of a play or book in a newspaper

explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to observe it, and a theatre write-up is a short published critique.

clue.text: Ungrammatical version of fewer directions from Bennett's Hilda

parts.note: using 'less' with a countable plural, where 'fewer' is correct, is the classic grammatical slip
ways are routes or directions

explanation.surface: A pedant's note on careless grammar about routes taken by a heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilda Lessways is the title heroine of the second Clayhanger novel by Arnold Bennett, so her surname is meant.

clue.text: "I would have thocht the thowless — hadna the smeddom left to interfere" (George Douglas, The House with Green Shutters)

definitions.text: "I would have thocht the thowless — hadna the smeddom left to interfere" (George Douglas, The House with Green Shutters)

parts.words: "I would have thocht the thowless — hadna the smeddom left to interfere" (George Douglas, The House with Green Shutters)
parts.note: a Scots quotation with a word dashed out: a Scots noun for a weary, worn-out drudge fits the gap

explanation.surface: A gossip in a Scottish town scoffs that a feeble character has no spirit left to meddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thowless' means listless and 'smeddom' means spirit or gumption in Scots; the missing word is a Scots term for a careworn, overburdened person.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots the word means a toilsome drudge or a weary, harassed person, fitting the spiritless figure in the quotation.

clue.text: A convert to Benson?

parts.note: points both to the apostle converted on the Damascus road and to the one-word title of a 1906 novel by E. F. Benson

explanation.surface: A question about someone won over by a writer named Benson.
explanation.walkthrough: Saul of Tarsus took a new name after his conversion; E. F. Benson used the same name as a novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle is Christianity's most famous convert, and Benson's novel bears his name.

clue.text: Worries concealed by resentment in roguish style

indicators.note: one word hidden inside another, so the worries sit within the resentment

parts.note: pique is a fit of wounded resentment
cares are worries

explanation.surface: Anxieties lurk beneath bitterness in a rascally manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealed by' is the container signal; 'in roguish style' is adjectival, as a picaresque novel follows a rascal's adventures.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish novel of rogue's adventures gave the term for fiction following a lovable rascal.

clue.text: Strange mania a girl reveals for reader's notes

indicators.note: something strange is out of the ordinary, so these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A girl's odd obsession shows in the jottings left by someone reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges the ten letters of MANIA A GIRL; 'reveals for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: These are comments scribbled in the edges of a page by someone working through a book.

clue.text: Bury opinions from meetings with biographer

parts.note: to inter is to bury a body
views are opinions

explanation.surface: A graveside debate about putting views to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sessions in which a subject answers a writer's questions are the raw material of many a life story.

clue.text: Seemingly not in Grishkin's wardrobe

parts.note: alludes to T. S. Eliot's 'Whispers of Immortality', where Grishkin's bust is described as 'Uncorseted'

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain lady apparently owns none of a type of garment.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliot writes that 'Uncorseted, her friendly bust / Gives promise of pneumatic bliss', so these garments seem absent from her clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The garments are stiffened, laced undergarments shaping the waist and bust, which Eliot's Grishkin goes without.

clue.text: Princess of France's witty attendant finds river ordinary, and salty

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps
O is an abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
saline means salty

explanation.surface: A courtier discovers a river that is plain and briny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finds' and 'and' are links. In Love's Labour's Lost the Princess of France is attended by three ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost, the sharp-tongued lady who mocks Berowne is one of the Princess's attendants.

clue.text: Journalist follows bird in elevated style

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other, so the journalist is placed at the end

parts.note: the stilt is a long-legged wading bird
ED is short for editor, a crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter tracks a wading bird with an air of grandeur.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff, pompous writing is said to be raised up as on poles, artificial and grand.

clue.text: Milton's work in rapid movement

parts.note: the companion poem to Il Penseroso, whose Italian title is also a musical term for a brisk tempo with the article in front

explanation.surface: A piece by the poet set to a lively tempo.
explanation.walkthrough: Allegro is the musical marking for a fast, cheerful pace; Milton's poem adds the Italian article and means 'the cheerful man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's 1645 pastoral poem celebrates mirth, and its title is the Italian for the happy man, a fast musical tempo.

clue.text: Flying heart doctors

parts.note: winged infant figures of love, pictured mending or piercing hearts, seen in Italian painting and sculpture

explanation.surface: Cardiac surgeons on an air ambulance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests medics in flight; the answer is the winged cupids of Renaissance art, who govern hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: These are little winged cupids, Italian for small loves, who take charge of lovers' feelings.

clue.text: Landor's friend got up with Sir Felix, Dickens scholar (6)

parts.note: rose is the past tense of rise, to get up
Sir Felix Aylmer, the English actor who also wrote books on Dickens

explanation.surface: Someone rises to join an actor knowledgeable about Victorian fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link; the extra '(6)' is printed in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Savage Landor's elegy mourns his young friend, the Hon. Rose Aylmer, who died in India.

clue.text: Priest featured in La Scala masterwork

indicators.note: something featured in a work appears within it, so the letters run inside these words

explanation.surface: A clergyman appears in a great opera at the Milan house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featured in' points to the letters running across 'Scala masterwork'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tibetan Buddhist monk or spiritual teacher holds the title.

clue.text: Composer carries little weight in the marketplace

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, so the weight sits within the marketplace

parts.note: a mart is a market
oz, the abbreviation for ounce, is a small weight

explanation.surface: A musician has little clout in commercial dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolfgang Amadeus of Salzburg wrote operas and symphonies, the classic example of a musical genius.

clue.text: A chooser of British poets, like Southey or Hazlitt

definitions.text: A chooser of British poets, like Southey or Hazlitt

parts.words: A chooser of British poets, like Southey or Hazlitt
parts.note: both men compiled anthologies with titles of the form 'Select British Poets', so each was a picker of verse

explanation.surface: A description of literary men as judges of poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Hazlitt's 1824 anthology was 'Select British Poets' and Southey edited a similar collection, so each acted as a picker.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who picks items for inclusion, as an anthologist picks poems.

clue.text: "… with the calce of egg shells, / white marble," (Ben Jonson, The Alchemist)

definitions.text: "… with the calce of egg shells, / white marble," (Ben Jonson, The Alchemist)

parts.words: "… with the calce of egg shells, / white marble," (Ben Jonson, The Alchemist)
parts.note: a quotation from Subtle's list of alchemical ingredients, with the missing word a soft white mineral

explanation.surface: A line from a Jacobean comedy listing alchemists' powders.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Alchemist, Subtle reels off his materials; the gap before 'with' is filled by a soft mineral used as a powder.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft magnesium silicate mineral, ground into powder, belongs in the alchemist's list beside chalky egg shell and marble.

clue.text: Go admire sort of symbol

indicators.note: to sort letters is to arrange them, so these are put into a new order

explanation.surface: An invitation to appreciate a kind of emblem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges the eight letters of GO ADMIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A written character that stands for an idea rather than a sound, as in Chinese script.

clue.text: A measure of ashes from Thomas Browne

definitions.text: A measure of ashes from Thomas Browne

parts.words: A measure of ashes from Thomas Browne
parts.note: nods to Browne's 'Hydriotaphia, Urn Burial', where he speaks of the quantity of ashes held in a funeral vessel

explanation.surface: A quantity of cremated remains mentioned by a seventeenth-century physician-writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Browne's treatise on ancient burial urns uses this word for as much as one funeral vessel holds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means as much as a burial vessel will contain, a usage Browne applied to cremated remains.

clue.text: Credit one manuscript value to The Professor character

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
I is the Roman numeral one
worth is value

explanation.surface: Assigning credit and worth to a manuscript about an academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. The Professor is Charlotte Brontë's first novel.
explanation.definitionFit: William Crimsworth narrates Charlotte Brontë's The Professor, teaching in Brussels.
